correctness.rationale: An explicit piecewise-triangular unit-Jacobian bijection couples interior volume measures. Sampling by layerwise-permuted uniform order statistics reduces every coordinate pair to a sorted uniform and a consecutive Dirichlet gap sum; exact first/second moments yield \(s_g(N-s_g-m_g)/((N+1)^2(N+2))\) for every within-layer covariance entry. Summation counts triples across distinct levels once, obtaining \(e_3\) exactly. Two-level coordinate reflection proves the positive case of congruence, inertia positivity excludes all others, and an exact balancing move proves sharp equality classes. Exact rational barycentric integration over 127 independently enumerated composition triangulations corroborates all formulas. No numerical extrapolation is used as proof.

originality.rationale: The source-family primary papers cover f-vectors/ordinal sums or unimodular equivalence, not exact volume-uniform second moments. A review of related available claim statements found only different invariants: a three-equal-layer mean-width asymptotic and rooted-tree intrinsic volumes. Targeted published-finding corpus and primary-literature searches for aliases and stronger statements revealed no implication of the \(e_3\) inertia identity, fixed-height sharp extremizers, or within-layer covariance law. Residual unindexed-moment priority risk remains.
residual_risks: Historical priority is not independently certified; an unindexed second-moment identity could cover some or all claims.

value.rationale: The volume-uniform centroidal inertia is an intrinsic Euclidean spatial-dispersion invariant that is not fixed by equality of Ehrhart polynomials. Its nonzero difference is a surprisingly simple symmetric function of maximal-ranked-poset layer sizes, gives a complete Euclidean congruence boundary and sharp extremal layer profiles, and admits a stronger covariance-block refinement. It provides a natural metric classification within a recognized family, not an arbitrary finite slice or unsupported numerical improvement.
